claims.text: Deliberately induced multi-element segregation at grain boundaries reduces grain-boundary energy relative to a random elemental distribution.
Multi-element grain-boundary segregation reduces the thermodynamic driving force for grain growth.
Multi-element grain-boundary segregation suppresses atomic diffusion at high temperature.
Tailoring local grain-boundary composition increases the energetic barrier for atomic jumps.
The increased atomic-jump barrier lowers vacancy-mediated diffusion.
Slower atomic diffusion minimizes grain growth and promotes microstructural stability.
Controlled multi-element grain-boundary segregation enhances structural stability in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Controlled multi-element grain-boundary segregation enhances chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Untreated high-entropy alloys can have random elemental site occupancy.
The elements in the baseline nanoalloy are randomly distributed across both grain interiors and grain boundaries.
Targeted annealing can be used to induce grain-boundary segregation.
Reduced grain-boundary energy causes a decrease in diffusion-driven phase nucleation.
Segregated samples will have lower atomic diffusion coefficients than random-distribution controls after identical high-temperature exposure.
Segregated samples will exhibit less grain growth than random-distribution controls after identical high-temperature exposure.
Segregated samples will sustain phase stability longer than random-distribution controls during high-temperature exposure.
The prediction is limited to nanoalloys in which grain-boundary-mediated diffusion is a dominant degradation pathway.
The magnitude of the stability improvement depends on elemental combinations, processing parameters, and microstructural characteristics.
Grain-boundary energy can be inferred sufficiently from microstructural evolution to serve as a falsification measurement.
